title: Doña Gracia Nasi
hook: a converso businesswoman who organized escapes for many

segments.voice: Yesterday, exiles settling in Istanbul and Salonika, with congregations named for home. Your line was another people opened the gate. Today, a woman who helped people get to those doors.

A merchant's letter goes out from a counting house in Antwerp. On paper, it is about pepper, cloth and credit. Underneath, it is about people: which family is ready to leave, which road over the Alps is safe this month, which agent in which city will hide them for a night and give them money for the next stage. The woman behind those letters was baptized, rich and watched. She was also running an escape route. Today, Doña Gracia Nasi.
screen: `A LETTER ABOUT PEPPER.` → `REALLY ABOUT PEOPLE.` → `A HIDDEN ESCAPE ROUTE.`

segments.voice: She was born into a family of New Christians in Portugal, the families we met two days ago, and raised with a Christian name, Beatriz de Luna. She married into a great trading house, the Mendes family, and after her husband and then his brother died, she ran the business herself. Her firm dealt in spices and banking across Europe. That network of ships, agents and credit became something else in her hands: a way out. Through her agents, New Christians from Portugal could travel north to Antwerp, then over the mountains into Italy, and on toward the Ottoman lands where they could live openly as Jews. She moved that way herself, through Antwerp, Venice and Ferrara, sometimes under arrest, sometimes in court battles over her fortune. Along the way she took up a Jewish name, Gracia Nasi, and in the end she reached Istanbul, where she lived openly as a Jew. People called her la Señora, the lady. Writers and scholars she supported praised her; Samuel Usque, whose book of consolation we met with Portugal, dedicated it to her. One Jewish story that resembles hers is Esther's: a woman at court hiding who she was, who is told that her place may be the very reason she is there. Mordecai says to her: "who knoweth whether thou art not come to royal estate for such a time as this?" Gracia Nasi had no crown. She had ledgers, ships and agents, and she used them the way Esther used the palace: for her people.
screen: `BORN A NEW CHRISTIAN.` · `A WIDOW RUNS THE FIRM.` · `TRADE ROUTES BECOME ESCAPE ROUTES.` · then, large: `FOR SUCH A TIME AS THIS.`

segments.voice: Gracia Nasi didn't invent a new tool; she turned the one in her hands. Look at your own, a phone full of contacts, a car, a spare room, a skill, a language, and ask quietly who it could help get somewhere safer, steadier or less alone.
Gracia Nasi. A businesswoman born into a New Christian family, who turned a trading network into an escape route and lived openly as a Jew. Today's word.
Your line: la señora. Ledgers and ships, turned into a way out. That's day nine hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Doña Gracia Nasi is remembered in Jewish communities as a rescuer and patron, and her story is often told alongside Esther's as a woman who used her position for her people.
